title: Financial-Aid Overflow Desk for New Loan Caps
one_liner: A managed service plus software that classifies programs as professional versus graduate, tracks lifetime caps and prevents mis-awards at small colleges' aid offices.
customer: Financial-aid directors and CFOs at small and mid-size, graduate-heavy private colleges and health-sciences schools.
problem: The July 1, 2026 regime capped grad loans at $20.5k a year and $100k total, gave only 11 'professional' programs $50k and $200k, and capped and prorated Parent PLUS by credit load. Final guidance came in May, vendors were not ready in August, and some disbursements ran 6 weeks late with no recourse. Errors create audit findings and student harm.
solution: An aid-regime desk: a program-classification dossier per program, cap tracking across borrowers including transfers, a Parent PLUS proration calculator, packaging letters, and a student-facing 'what you can borrow and alternatives' guide (private loan comparison, employer sponsorship, payment plan). Add a late-disbursement bridge program and audit-ready records.
why_now: This is the first aid cycle under the new rules. A pending healthcare-association lawsuit (December 2026 suspension deadline) means rules could change again, and vendors lag.
revenue_model: $25-90k per institution per year depending on graduate enrollment, plus bridge-loan fees per student.
non_obvious_insight: Every rule change is a compliance tax that lands hardest on small offices. The vendor lag is a 12-18 month window in which a service desk becomes embedded in the workflow and later converts to software.
first_30_days: Contact 20 small graduate-heavy colleges (nursing, counseling). Offer a $5k cap-readiness audit reviewing 100 student files. Publish a plain-English cap guide to generate leads and sign 3.

title: Blue Tarp Index: Adjuster Ground Truth for ILS
one_liner: A subscription that sells cat-bond and reinsurance investors what veteran field adjusters can see in the first 10 days after a disaster, before any model or carrier report exists.
customer: ILS funds, cat bond trading desks, reinsurance-broker analytics teams, and hedge-fund or equity analysts covering Florida, Gulf and California-exposed carriers. Roughly $30k-$120k per year per team.
problem: Post-event loss estimates swing wildly (Milton was pegged anywhere from a few tens of billions up, and cat-bond implied-loss marks moved daily) and settle slowly. The cat bond market is now about $65.6B outstanding after a record $17.6B of H1 2026 issuance, and most of that capital marks to modeler guesses and carrier press releases. Investors have no structured ground truth for the variables that decide severity: how many roofs really failed, whether demand surge is 10% or 40%, and whether contractors can staff repairs at all.
solution: A vetted panel of 60-150 independent veteran cat adjusters files 10-minute standardized mobile observations on publicly visible conditions only: blue-tarp density per 100 roofs on sampled blocks, roofing debris and dumpster counts, mystery-shopped contractor and tarp-crew quotes ($/sq, lead times), hotel and RV occupancy, and adjuster deployment density. Outputs are an event dashboard, a 'Blue Tarp Index' and a demand-surge index within 72 hours to 10 days, a weekly note, and paid expert calls. Hard rule, reviewed by counsel: no claim-file, policyholder or carrier-confidential information, only public observation and market pricing, aggregated and anonymized.
why_now: Cat bond and ILS capital hit records in 2026, with over $120B of ILS capacity, so more money is exposed to event-loss uncertainty than ever. Claims-adjuster employment fell about 21% year over year through May 2026 as carriers automate, which leaves a large pool of experienced people who need income and are cheap to recruit. The very quiet 2026 Atlantic season (no hurricane until at least Sept 11) gives a scrappy team time to build and back-test before the next event. Wildfire, hail and flood events also count as live tests.
revenue_model: Annual subscription tiers ($25k signal-only, $60k with expert calls, $120k+ bespoke event coverage), per-event pay-per-call expert sessions, and paid retrospective studies. Adjusters get $75-$150 per completed field report plus a revenue share pool. Gross margin is high because the data is field labor, not infrastructure.
non_obvious_insight: Models price wind and exposure, but severity in the real world is set by contractor capacity: how many roofers, tarp crews and drying crews physically exist within 200 miles. An adjuster feels that constraint on day 4 because they cannot get a tarp crew to a house, and nobody in finance measures it. Tarps are also what the policy pays for first, so their density is a fast, visible proxy for claim frequency. The hypothesis is testable by back-testing against Helene, Milton and the LA fires.
first_30_days: Recruit 25 laid-off or semi-retired cat adjusters from cat-adjuster Facebook groups, adjuster forums and LinkedIn. Draft the observation protocol and a counsel-approved compliance memo. Run a retrospective 'what we would have told you on day 7' study on Helene/Milton and the Jan 2025 LA fires using panel memory, public imagery and contractor pricing archives. Publish a free sample note, send it to 15 ILS portfolio managers and 5 broker analytics heads, and aim for 2-3 paid pilots ($15-25k) that include the retro study as a deliverable, with the first live test on spring 2027 hail or a wildfire.

title: Steeple Sites: Church Land for Satellite Ground Stations
one_liner: Master-lease deals with denominations to host satellite ground stations, gateways and RF sensors on steeples and surplus church land, sold to operators as a ready-made site portfolio.
customer: Ground-station-as-a-service networks, smallsat IoT and EO operators, and direct-to-cell or broadband constellation operators needing gateways. Congregations and dioceses are paid as hosts.
problem: Launch has flooded orbit (321 launches, 4,517 satellites deployed in 2025, about 10,400 Starlinks), and carrier partnerships are multiplying, so downlink capacity, gateways and RF-quiet sites are a constraint. Site acquisition is slow, one farm or roof at a time. Meanwhile congregations own tall, zoning-friendly structures and acreage, monthly attendance is stuck at about 33%, and many boards need rental income or surplus-property solutions.
solution: Negotiate master-lease templates with denominational property boards (diocesan or conference trustees). Pre-screen sites for line of sight, RF noise, power, fiber and zoning, and package them into portfolios by latitude and orbit. Partner integrators handle permitting and install, and congregations get a share.
why_now: The spectrum land-grab settled (EchoStar's $23B sale to AT&T closed in July 2026, and the $17B sale to SpaceX), MNO satellite deals are multiplying, and every country-level service needs terrestrial infrastructure. Congregation attendance has plateaued at a low level, so property decisions are live.
revenue_model: A $5-15k site-acquisition fee per signed site paid by the operator, 15-20% of lease revenue for the life of the lease, and install margin. Congregations target $6-24k per year (to be validated).
non_obvious_insight: The tower industry already proved steeples are leasable, tall, permitted and governed by a few trustees, but satellite site teams chase farmland. One denomination negotiation can unlock hundreds of sites, and a closing parish is a seller with time pressure.
first_30_days: Pick one diocese or conference with rural clusters and pitch a pro-bono pilot lease template. Screen 30 sites from imagery, and approach 3 ground-network or IoT operators with a shortlist for a country where they lack coverage. Charge a $2-5k site-survey fee for a 10-site report as the first revenue.

title: Owner-Statement Auditor for Landlords With Property Managers
one_liner: Forward your property manager's monthly owner statements and get back the line items that don't add up: repairs with no invoice, charges on the wrong property, reserve draws that hide shortfalls, and true days vacant.
customer: Self-directed small investors with 2 to 30 doors who pay a third-party property manager, especially out-of-state owners. A second tier is the bookkeepers and CPAs who serve them and would white-label it.
problem: Every PM uses a different statement format, a different definition of 'net to owner' and a different fee schedule. Owners cannot tell whether a $400 repair really cost $900. Fees are often a percentage of the project, so the PM benefits from a bigger job. Thorough reconciliation takes 5 to 10 minutes per property per month, so most owners only glance at the deposit. Owners with several PMs end up rebuilding everything in QuickBooks or Excel by hand.
solution: An email-in service with no new PM software. The owner forwards PDF or CSV statements, or connects the PM portal export. Document extraction normalizes each statement into one chart of accounts. The owner also uploads the PM agreement, and the service extracts its fee terms and approval thresholds. Rules then flag: charges with no invoice; repeated repairs just under the approval threshold; the same vendor billed across properties for work meant for one; reserve movements that mask a shortfall; late-fee handling that differs from the contract; and fees booked in the wrong month. It also computes true days vacant (turn time included) as opposed to the 'days on market' PMs report, plus maintenance cost per door and the share of work orders closed on the first visit. Output is a one-page monthly report and a ready-to-send dispute email. An optional human bookkeeper review is the upsell.
why_now: Sept 2026 BiggerPockets threads show owners asking these exact questions with no tool that answers them. Landlord banking tools (Baselane, RentRedi) still 'aren't really bookkeeping', as one thread puts it. Extracting structured data from messy PM statement PDFs became cheap and reliable with current document-AI models. That turns a manual forensic accounting service into a $9-per-door product.
revenue_model: $9 per door per month, or $99 per property per year. A one-time $199 backfill audit of the trailing 12 months acts as the lead magnet and first revenue. A bookkeeper and CPA white-label plan at about $49 per client per month. The audit could later be paired with recovery: for any overcharge that gets refunded, take 15%.
non_obvious_insight: Owners are not asking for another PM platform. They want a neutral second set of eyes, and PMs will never build one because they are the party being checked. Evidence: 'How do you verify your PM net deposit matches the statement each month?' (19 replies) lists wrong-property charges, repairs with no invoice, and reserve adjustments that absorb shortfalls, at 5-10 minutes per property (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/899/topics/1293899-how-do-you-verify-your-pm-net-deposit-matches-the-statement-each-month). 'Every PM seems to send a different statement format, a different definition of net to owner' (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/963/topics/1292833-owners-with-multiple-pms-how-do-you-keep-one-clean-view-across-statements). Owners can't verify whether a $400 repair needed $900, and 'days on market is not days vacant' (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/963/topics/1301673-what-actually-keeps-out-of-state-landlords-up-at-night). A repair-transparency survey quote reads: 'I couldn't tell which line items were fair and which were padded' (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/52/topics/1302340-small-landlords-with-a-pm-2-minute-survey-on-fees-and-repair-estimates).
first_30_days: Week 1: reply in the threads above and offer a free 12-month statement audit to 10 owners in exchange for anonymized statements. Build the audit by hand with a spreadsheet, an extraction prompt and a rules checklist. Weeks 2 to 3: deliver the audits, and use the discrepancies found as case studies. Week 4: convert to the $199 backfill and $9-per-door subscription, and pitch three real-estate bookkeepers on the white-label plan. Target: 10 paying owners and 2 bookkeeper partners.

title: Approved-Protocol Envelope Guard for AI-Directed Labs
one_liner: Middleware that turns an institution's biosafety approval into machine-readable limits and stops any agent-proposed experiment that falls outside them before a robot runs it, leaving an insurer-grade black-box record.
customer: Biosafety officers and lab directors at universities, CROs and AI-native biotechs that let agents propose or modify protocols. Later, insurers and MGAs who need trace data. The direct buyer is the lab or institution.
problem: Institutional Biosafety Committees approve specific organisms, agents, quantities and containment levels, but agents now propose edits on the fly (a new strain, a higher concentration, a substitute reagent). There is no standard sign-off model, since CDC/WHO frameworks predate autonomous systems, and records must separate AI proposal, human edit and robot execution. ISO's generative-AI exclusion (CG 40 47 01 26) took effect in January 2026 and Verisk is weighing agentic exclusions, so the resulting liability is increasingly uninsured.
solution: Ingest the approved protocol (IBC registration, BSL level, permitted agents and amounts, IACUC limits) as a machine-readable envelope. Check every agent-proposed step against it before execution. Anything out of envelope pauses the run and goes to the biosafety officer with a diff. All proposals, human edits and executions are logged tamper-evidently. Each run yields an 'envelope compliance report' for the IBC file and, later, for underwriters.
why_now: Anthropic's wet lab and similar setups (about 950 agents on one discovery) show agents can generate far more proposals than human reviewers can read. The FDA's September 2026 nonclinical-methods rule raises scrutiny of AI-run studies. Carriers are excluding what they cannot model, so trace holders can price the risk.
revenue_model: SaaS per lab or robot ($1-3K/month), enterprise deployments for CROs, and later an MGA or data-licensing arrangement in which underwriters pay for envelope-compliance telemetry or grant premium credits.
non_obvious_insight: The real buyer is the overloaded biosafety officer, not the scientist, and the hard part is translating IBC PDFs into constraints rather than the AI. Whoever holds the runtime traces becomes the pricing authority for agentic lab risk, and model labs cannot be that neutral party.
first_30_days: Interview 15 biosafety officers through the ABSA community. Ship a read-only 'diff checker' that takes an IBC protocol PDF plus an agent's experiment plan and flags out-of-envelope steps. Sell 3 paid pilots ($2-5K) to AI-native labs and one university core. Use the pilot logs to draft an insurer-ready report format.

title: Advancement Ledger for Parents Funding Jobless Kids
one_liner: A living ledger plus a state-specific estate addendum that records what Boomer parents advance to struggling adult children, so the inheritance later comes out fair and siblings do not end up in court.
customer: Parents aged 65-80 with $500K-$5M estates and two or more adult children, at least one of whom is unemployed or underemployed. Channel: estate attorneys, elder-law firms and RIAs, who white-label it. Payers: parents ($199 setup plus $12-20/mo), firms ($500/mo white label) or RIAs (per-household fee).
problem: The AI hiring freeze (NY Fed: recent-grad underemployment about 42%) turns Mom and Dad into the bank of last resort. Rent, tuition, car and 'bridge loans' flow unevenly to siblings, undocumented and undecided as gift, loan or advancement against inheritance. Decades later, executors and trustees face contested history and estate litigation, and families break. Wealth advisors say family meetings are essential, yet nobody tracks advances.
solution: Parents log each advance in a simple app and tag it as gift, loan or advancement. The child e-acknowledges it. Optional interest at the AFR turns it into a formal promissory note. The system flags amounts near gift-tax-return thresholds (annual exclusion about $19K). It produces a running equalization statement the attorney can attach to a will or trust with a state-specific 'hotchpot' clause. An annual sibling-transparent 'family statement' replaces secrecy. Repayment or forgiveness schedules kick in when a child gets re-employed.
why_now: Millions of 22-35-year-olds face a low-hire market while Gen X and Millennial heirs are about to receive trillions (Cerulli: Gen X about $14T in the next decade). Federal student-loan caps reportedly tightened from July 2026 (verify), pushing more tuition onto family money. With a higher federal estate exemption (reportedly about $15M per person from 2026, verify), fewer estates are tax-driven and more are conflict-driven, so fairness documentation is now the main planning value.
revenue_model: $199 'Fair Share Package' (memo, ledger, 45-minute attorney review). $12-20/mo subscription. Attorney and RIA white label at $500/mo per firm or a per-household fee. Later: paid mediation add-on when siblings disagree.
non_obvious_insight: The AI jobs shock will show up in probate court a decade before it shows up in most statistics. Unequal parental support is the seed of the next generation of estate fights, and equalization is a data problem (a ledger), not a legal one. Parents will pay real money to keep their kids from fighting after they die.
first_30_days: With two friendly estate attorneys, draft an advancement memo and equalization clause for two states. Put up a landing page aimed at parents searching 'paying rent for my 26-year-old' and post in personal-finance and parenting communities. Sell the $199 package with a manual spreadsheet ledger to the first 25 families, then build the app around what they actually log. Ask 10 elder-law attorneys to co-present at seminars.

title: Walkable Childhood Homes for Memory Care
one_liner: Generate explorable 3D versions of a person's childhood street, lost home or homeland from a few photos and stories, delivered on a TV or tablet for memory care, hospice and diaspora families.
customer: Memory-care and assisted-living communities (activity budgets), hospices and adult children, paying $250-600 per scene or $300-600 a month per community.
problem: Reminiscence is among the best-supported non-drug interventions for dementia and late-life low mood, but the props are still photos and music. Existing VR programs offer generic 'visit Paris' content, not personal places. Immigrants, refugees and the bereaved have no visual way back to a home that no longer exists.
solution: A studio workflow: family interview intake, photo and archival-map collection, a world-model pipeline that builds an era-appropriate walkable scene, and a docent mode where staff or grandchildren ask 'what was on this corner?'. Human artists finalize each scene to remove uncanny or distressing artifacts, and a gentle mode limits sensory intensity.
why_now: Generative world models released in 2025 (Google's Genie 3, World Labs' Marble and similar) can create persistent, explorable scenes from a handful of images. That cuts the cost of a personalized environment from thousands of dollars to well under $100 of compute.
revenue_model: Per-scene fees, community subscriptions for scene libraries and refreshes, hospice partnerships, and a consumer gift channel for diaspora families.
non_obvious_insight: Reminiscence works best when it is specific and shared, and personalization used to cost too much. The most valuable scenes are not beautiful cities but the ordinary corner, kitchen and street a person actually lived on.
first_30_days: Offer 10 memory-care communities three free scenes each, generated from residents' family photos. Track engagement and agitation logs with staff, then sell five-scene packs at $500 and add one hospice partner.

title: Purge-to-Spool Toll Recycler for Print Farms
one_liner: A mail-in service that turns multicolour purge waste and failed prints into laser-checked, guaranteed-diameter filament, so print farms get spools back without owning or babysitting a $1,200-$1,700 recycling rig.
customer: Print farms and Etsy print sellers running Bambu-style multicolour printers, maker spaces, schools and STEM programmes that produce kilograms of purge and failed prints monthly. Payer is the print-farm owner.
problem: Multicolour printing generates heavy purge waste, and existing recycling only pays in store credit. The DIY route (Creality's shredder plus filament maker) has diameter, jam and ROI risks that backers already worry about.
solution: Prepaid bins ship to the customer, who tosses in purge, supports and failed prints (same-polymer sorting only: PLA, PETG). The central facility shreds, dries, extrudes and spools with an inline laser micrometer, and returns a share of the weight as certified filament (for example a 1.75mm +/-0.03mm 'galaxy' random-colour spool). The remainder is sold as premium recycled filament. Customers see kg diverted and a certificate for 'green' Etsy claims.
why_now: Multicolour printing exploded (each Bambu Cube-style multicolour test can burn about 70 g of purge), and Creality's Filament Maker M1 and Shredder R1 hit its Indiegogo goal in 16 minutes and raised $6.8M from 5,320 backers, so waste is a felt problem. The first real-world tests show the DIY loop is not yet dependable, leaving a gap for a professional processor.
revenue_model: $3/kg intake fee (or pay-per-bin at $115 as Printerior's prepaid bins do), plus margin on selling recycled spools at $12-18/kg, plus a B2B subscription of $79-$199/mo for farms wanting monthly pickup and returns.
non_obvious_insight: Hobbyists backed a $649-$1,699 recycler, but the machine's own pre-production data shows why a service beats owning one. One reviewer measured filament diameter varying 1.78 mm to 1.58 mm across a single spool, and a complex print jammed at 97% recycled content. Creality itself recommends a 1:1 blend, and backers question ROI after electricity, failures and maintenance (https://makers101.com/creality-filament-maker-m1-shredder-r1-live-tracker/, raise figure of $6,816,733 from 5,320 backers; note that https://www.tcf.team/blog/q1-2026-crowdfunding-report reports a different $36M figure, so the exact total is uncertain, but demand is clear either way). Existing recyclers pay only points (Printerior: 280 points/kg redeemable for filament, and it requires sorted PLA/PLA+/PETG, https://printeriordesigns.com/pages/recycling), yet Printerior sells $114.99 prepaid bins, so people already pay to dispose responsibly. Nobody offers cash or spec-guaranteed spools back.
first_30_days: Buy a used 1.75mm extruder line, a shredder and a laser micrometer (about $6-10K) or rent time at a plastics co-op. Recruit 5 local print farms and 2 school maker labs as free pilots. Run 200 kg through, test diameter and print reliability in a 1:1 virgin blend, and photograph results. Then open pre-orders for prepaid bins ($115) and monthly pickup on the Bambu and Etsy-seller subreddits.

title: Group Apprenticeship Employer for Data-Center Electricians
one_liner: An Australian-style group training organization that employs apprentices and rents them to small electrical and plumbing contractors, absorbing the paperwork, wage risk and poaching risk.
customer: Small and mid-size electrical, plumbing and HVAC contractors (5-50 staff) in data-center and construction-boom metros; apprentices, including underemployed college grads.
problem: Electricians have about 72.7k openings a year, boosted by data-center demand, but the 4-5 year path is bottlenecked by employer sponsors and pre-apprenticeship screening. Small contractors cannot carry multi-year risk, admin and classroom scheduling, and apprentices are poached after year one or two. Meanwhile 42% of recent grads are underemployed and have no route in.
solution: The group sponsor is the registered-apprenticeship sponsor and employer of record. It screens and recruits, pays wages and workers' comp, rotates apprentices across host contractors, schedules related instruction with a community college or JATC (up to 49% of instruction can be outsourced to employers or unions under the new apprenticeship rules), and bills hosts hourly. Market a career-changer track to laid-off grads.
why_now: AI data-center construction is pulling electricians while AI is closing entry-level white-collar doors, creating both demand and a motivated recruit pool. Workforce Pell gives apprenticeship-linked programs a fast lane, making college partners eager.
revenue_model: A 20-30% markup over apprentice wage cost billed to host contractors (about 15-20% gross margin, staffing-style), plus state apprenticeship incentives and college partnership fees.
non_obvious_insight: Contractors do not lack applicants; they lack appetite for multi-year risk and administration. Splitting the employer role from the host job site removes the constraint, as group training organizations did in Australia.
first_30_days: Choose one data-center metro. Sign 5 small contractors to LOIs for 10 apprentice seats. Partner with an existing IEC or ABC chapter for registration and compliance. Recruit 30 candidates from local underemployed grads and start an 8-week evening pre-apprenticeship course.

title: The Recorder's Rulebook: Avalara for the Recording Counter
one_liner: A verified, machine-readable rulebook and fee oracle for every recording jurisdiction, with a preflight checker that tells you a document will be rejected before you send it.
customer: Small and mid-size title and escrow agencies, estate-planning and real estate attorneys, HOA and property managers, lenders' closing teams, and later closing-software and e-recording platforms that embed the API. Counties get listed free.
problem: There are roughly 3,600 recording jurisdictions, each with its own margins, font sizes, notary wording, parcel-ID format, cover sheets, per-page fees, surcharges and transfer taxes. Those rules sit on stale county web pages and in clerks' heads. Rejections delay closings two to seven days, burn recorder staff time on every bounce, and wrong fee estimates create TRID tolerance problems for lenders. Fees also keep moving as counties backfill shrinking recording revenue (Wayne County MI has floated a $30 fee increase, Montana raised per-page fees, and other counties report seven-figure losses tied to fee changes).
solution: A crowd-verified rulebook per county and document type. A PDF preflight scans geometry (margins, fonts, blank space), notary block completeness, legal description, APN format and preparer and return-to fields, and returns specific fixes. A to-the-penny fee and transfer-tax calculator handles every surcharge. A change log tracks statute changes and effective dates (many take effect July 1 or January 1). Each county gets a one-click quarterly 'attest my page' link, which clerks will use because every rejection costs them 15-30 minutes plus postage. Start as a free 'will this be rejected?' web checker to collect users, then sell API access.
why_now: Recording volumes have been depressed since 2022 and counties are raising fees, which makes fee tables stale. Remote online notarization and e-recording put far more documents in front of closers who have never met the county's quirks. Title staff attrition means fewer people who just know the rules. Vision-capable LLMs make geometry and notary-block checks cheap for the first time.
revenue_model: $1-$3 per preflight check plus $99-$499/month tiers for agencies. Per-call API pricing for closing platforms and e-recording vendors, and a data license for lenders needing accurate recording-fee and transfer-tax estimates.
non_obvious_insight: Clerks reject because the stamp is a legal act, not because we are picky. The top ten rejection reasons are identical everywhere, but the thresholds differ, and most bounces come from occasional submitters (attorneys, HOA managers, individuals), not the big title companies that already have local runners. The moat is not software, it is the boring verified dataset, and clerks will help you build it because they are the ones who suffer from the bounces.
first_30_days: Pick one state with an active recorders' association and build the full rulebook for 25 counties by phone and web, with a clerk sign-off on each. Ship the free checker, promote it through the association newsletter and estate-planning attorney groups, and convert the heaviest users to a $99/month plan. Approach a closing-software partner program once you have about 200 active users.

title: Apprentice Athlete: Injury-Proofing the Skilled Trades
one_liner: An 8-week pre-apprenticeship that conditions and movement-screens new electricians, plumbers and pipefitters so they survive the first two years.
customer: Joint apprenticeship training centers (IBEW/NECA, UA, IEC, ABC), community-college trade programs, and the workers' comp carriers and brokers behind contractors. Contractors pay per placed apprentice.
problem: Electricians have about 72.7k openings a year (data-center demand) and plumbers about 42k, but the 4-5 year apprenticeship path is bottlenecked by employer sponsors and weak pre-apprenticeship screening. Overexertion and strain injuries are consistently a leading cause of lost-time injuries and feed early attrition. Many entrants are sedentary career-changers, including displaced white-collar grads (42% of recent grads are underemployed).
solution: 'Apprentice Athlete' runs 3 sessions a week for 8 weeks in existing gyms, taught by athletic trainers and strength coaches. It uses trade-specific drills (overhead conduit work, ladder and pipe carries, crawlspace mobility, grip endurance), phone-video or cheap-wearable movement screens, and an injury-prevention curriculum. Completion, not a fitness score, earns JATC pre-apprenticeship credit and can slot in as a short program eligible for Workforce Pell where approved. It is structured as training rather than a hiring screen, to stay clear of ADA limits.
why_now: Workforce Pell launched July 1, 2026 but only 5 programs are approved. Apprenticeship-linked programs get a fast lane, and up to 49% of instruction can be delivered by employers or unions. Data-center demand is pulling electricians, and AI-exposed grads are pivoting to trades. Phone pose-estimation and cheap wearables are now good enough to measure movement quality.
revenue_model: $400-800 per apprentice per cohort paid by contractor, JATC or Pell/WIOA funds. A $100-200k pilot contract with a comp carrier tied to premium credits. Then per-seat licensing to gyms and trainers who run the program (they keep 60-70%).
non_obvious_insight: The trades treat the body as a consumable, while sports treat it as an appreciating asset. Comp carriers already have loss runs showing injuries cluster in the first 24 months, so a $600 conditioning program pays back if it prevents one strain claim per few dozen apprentices. Trade schools cannot have that ROI conversation, but insurers can.
first_30_days: Partner with one IEC/ABC chapter or a community-college trades program. Run a 6-week pilot for 20 career-changers using phone-video screening and a $50 tracker. Log attendance, attrition and minor injuries against the prior cohort. Take the numbers to the contractors' workers' comp broker to negotiate a premium-credit pilot.

title: Stablecoin Cash-Out Float for Corner Shops
one_liner: Stablecoins made sending money nearly free, so the scarce thing is cash at the last mile, and the margin goes to whoever finances the agents.
customer: Pharmacies, tiendas and kiosks that act as cash-out agents in Colombia, Mexico, Argentina and Nigeria, plus the stablecoin remittance and wallet apps that need them.
problem: A $200 US-to-Colombia transfer costs $12.13 on legacy rails versus about $0.01 in stablecoins, but recipients still want local cash. Small agents run out of float and refuse large withdrawals.
solution: A float-management app that shows each agent's cash position, advances intraday float against next-day USDC settlement and routes recipients to agents with liquidity. The wedge is 100 pharmacies on one remittance corridor for a single anchor partner.
why_now: Nigeria opened a stablecoin sandbox (Aug 12) and Kenya passed digital-currency legislation (Aug 6). Yellow Card is hiring in LatAm and SEA, and Felix has processed $8B over WhatsApp.
revenue_model: A 1-1.5% spread on float turnover plus a per-payout fee from the remitter.
non_obvious_insight: As stablecoin transfer fees go to zero, the margin migrates to the last ten metres of physical cash. This is cash logistics dressed up as fintech.
first_30_days: Sign one wallet or remittance partner as anchor and raise a roughly $50k float line from a debt fund. Onboard 20 pharmacies in one city.

title: Data Centers Fund Their Host Utility's Leak Repairs
one_liner: A turnkey program where a data-center developer pays to cut real water losses in the host utility's own system and gets a signed, metered, same-source volume to show regulators and neighbors.
customer: Data-center developers and colo operators fighting permit resistance (Cheyenne, Ohio, New York, Texas), plus the small and mid-size host utilities that receive the repairs. The developer pays.
problem: Insiders think 'water positive' means wetland or agricultural offsets in some other watershed. Locals and regulators now want physical relief on the same source in the same year. Meanwhile many small utilities lose 20-30% of what they treat, and can't fund repairs.
solution: Run an AWWA-style water audit of the host utility. Rank repairs by gallons saved per dollar (main breaks, service leaks, failed valves and meters). Fund local crews and verify the savings with district-metered-area flow data. Deliver a signed 'verified gallons saved' report to both the utility and the permitting file. The utility gets capacity to serve the new load without new supply.
why_now: Texas is making data-center non-reporting a crime and a bar to permits. Ohio scrapped its general discharge permit after more than 7,000 comments, New York has a moratorium, and Cheyenne revoked a permit. Australia's planned standards explicitly cover funding extra water infrastructure. Developers need mitigation that neighbors can verify.
revenue_model: 10-15% program-management fee on repair spend, margin on crew contracts, and a performance bonus per verified 1,000 gallons saved. A $15-25k paid feasibility study is the door-opener.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest same-source gallon is one the utility already treated and lost. This turns the data center from the utility's rival for water into its capital source, and 'water positive' gets judged by neighbors and permitting boards, not by sustainability reports.
first_30_days: Use public loss-audit filings (Texas, Georgia and California require them, in my understanding) to rank utilities near contested or pending data-center projects by real losses per connection. Write a 10-page 'loss-to-offset' report on three of them. Send it to the developers, and to the utilities as a free mailer. Aim for one paid feasibility study within 30 days.

title: Court-Rules MCP Server With a Deadline Warranty
one_liner: Effective-dated, human-verified court rules, judge standing orders and deadline math for one state at a time, exposed to any AI agent, with fee credits if a computed deadline is wrong.
customer: Solo and small firms (5 or fewer attorneys) in personal injury, family, criminal defense and landlord-tenant who already run Clio or MyCase and are starting to use Claude or ChatGPT agents. Later, legal-AI vendors that buy the rule set by API.
problem: Missed deadlines are among the most common malpractice claims (background knowledge, verify). General models know case law roughly but not this county's local rules, this judge's standing order (including AI-use certifications), or this year's fee schedule. The rules live as PDFs across thousands of court sites and change constantly, and big-firm docketing systems are priced and built for large firms.
solution: Start with one state pack, for example Texas civil. It holds statutes of limitation, civil procedure, local rules of the top counties and judge standing orders, each effective-dated with a hashed source PDF. MCP tools such as compute_deadline(event, court, date) and check_filing(court, judge, doc_type) return the date, the rule cites and a confidence flag. A deterministic engine does the date math (no LLM arithmetic), paid legal editors verify the high-use rules, and change alerts go out. A small warranty (fee credit plus capped reimbursement) backs the deadline output.
why_now: 8am's MyCase says 60+ firms, mostly 5 or fewer attorneys, adopted its Claude MCP connector (73 actions) in the first month, so small firms are now consuming practice tools through agents. Case law is open and the model is free, but local procedure is not in any frontier legal product.
revenue_model: $79-149/month per firm per state pack, an API license of $2-10k/month for legal-AI vendors, and a premium warranty tier.
non_obvious_insight: When the model is free and the corpus is open, the scarce asset is authoritative, effective-dated local procedure with a liability wrapper. Nobody can warrant an LLM's legal reasoning, but a rules engine plus editorial verification is exactly where a warranty is underwritable.
first_30_days: Pick one state and one practice area. Hand-build the 300 highest-frequency rules with two contract paralegals (about $8-10k), ship a free MCP server, and recruit 15 firms through a state solo and small-firm bar list. Charge $99/month after the trial, publish an accuracy audit, and keep the warranty to a $500 credit until loss data exists.

title: AI-Off Proficiency Checks for Clinicians
one_liner: E.M. Forster's The Machine Stops and Asimov's The Feeling of Power turned into recurrent, pilot-style checks that measure whether clinicians still perform well when the AI is switched off.
customer: GI and radiology group practices, hospital medical staff offices (ongoing professional practice evaluation and credentialing), physician-owned malpractice carriers seeking premium-credit evidence, and residency programs.
problem: Routine AI assistance may erode unaided skill. A 2025 Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology study of 19 experienced endoscopists in Poland found adenoma detection in non-AI colonoscopies fell from 28.4% to 22.4% after AI exposure (the study is observational and has been contested). No one measures unaided proficiency, unlike pilots' manual-flying currency, and outages or out-of-distribution cases will expose the gap.
solution: A quarterly, 25-minute, blinded and timed case set (videos and images with expert ground truth) delivered with AI overlays disabled. Scores are benchmarked against each clinician's own baseline and peer cohort, with drift alerts, targeted micro-drills, and a certificate for credentialing files and insurers. Add an AI-outage drill for departments (tabletop plus live). Start with colonoscopy, then extend to mammography and other AI-assisted reads.
why_now: AI computer-aided detection is now routine in colonoscopy and mammography. The deskilling study made the risk concrete and quotable. Malpractice carriers and hospital counsel are looking for defensible evidence, and the Joint Commission already requires ongoing professional practice evaluation.
revenue_model: $600-1,500 per clinician per year, carrier-funded programs paid per insured group, and enterprise licenses for health systems.
non_obvious_insight: Sell it as insurance evidence and credentialing paperwork, not education. Aviation shows regulators and insurers accept currency requirements once a failure mode is measured. The pre- and post-adoption unaided performance record is also what a hospital will need to defend an AI-related malpractice case, so buyers are motivated to start their baseline now.
first_30_days: License public polyp-video datasets and recruit two GI academic advisors to write ground truth. Build 10 case sets and pilot free for eight weeks with two GI groups. Pitch one physician-owned malpractice carrier on a premium credit for participating groups, then charge about $900 per clinician per year.

title: Waiver-Funded Home Modification Back Office and Factoring
one_liner: Handle the prior-authorization paperwork and advance payment for small contractors who do ramps and bathroom retrofits funded by Medicaid waivers and VA grants.
customer: Small accessibility and remodeling contractors (3-15 employees) in states with waiver home-modification benefits, plus case managers and AAAs who can't find bidders.
problem: Senior housing supply is stuck through 2030, so aging in place is structurally favored and home mods are the cheapest fix. But waiver and VA HISA funding needs OT assessments, multiple bids, packets, inspections and 60-120 day payment, so good contractors avoid it. Approved seniors can't find anyone to do the work.
solution: A back office that prepares the packet (OT evaluation scheduling, standard scope, photos, bids, permits), tracks approval, submits invoices, and advances 85-90% of payment within five days against the approved authorization. A network directory shows case managers which contractors are ready to bid.
why_now: 41 states have HCBS waitlists over 600k, so states favor cheap home-based solutions over $115k-a-year nursing home stays. Medicaid cuts and 15-month waits add pressure, while 80+ growth means demand for mods is up.
revenue_model: 3-5% packet fee, a 1.5-3% factoring spread, and a platform fee from states or MCOs for a ready-to-bid contractor pool.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for funded home modifications is contractor cash flow and paperwork, not consumer demand or budget. Fixing the contractor's experience creates supply where the money already exists.
first_30_days: In one state, recruit five contractors and process 10 packets. Secure a small credit line from a CDFI or SBA lender to fund advances, then approach the state's HCBS case management office.

title: Betting Profit-and-Loss Statements for Credit Unions
one_liner: Turn a member's bank ACH data into an 'investment-style' betting P&L (what they recovered per dollar deposited) and optional spending guardrails, licensed per member to credit unions and neobanks.
customer: Community banks, credit unions with young or college-town memberships, and neobanks, paying $0.25-0.60 per member per month. A free consumer version targets Gen Z bettors and their worried parents or partners.
problem: Online betting and prediction-market use is surging among the young. In June-July 2026 first-time users were about 3x January levels. Gen Z and Millennials were 88% of activity (Gen Z 48%). Bettors recovered under 75 cents per dollar sent to platforms. 23% of sports bettors bet daily and 34% weekly. Households that bet had a median deposit balance of only 59% of non-bettors'. Most of these users do not think of themselves as gamblers: 20% of respondents call sports betting a type of investment, Gen Z is about twice as likely to, and buying prediction-market event contracts is more likely to be called an investment than sports betting is.
solution: A detector that classifies ACH and card flows to sportsbooks, sweepstakes casinos and event-contract exchanges, using a maintained list of originator and descriptor names. It produces a plain 'Your realized return: -27%' statement in the vocabulary bettors already use (returns, cost basis), with a monthly summary and opt-in deposit caps or a cooling-off freeze. A parent, partner or co-guardian mode makes it useful for Gen Z members who live at home. The consumer version is a free upload-your-statement tool that generates a shareable 'what's your recovery ratio' card, which doubles as the top of the funnel for credit-union licenses.
why_now: Prediction markets went mainstream in 2026 and the FIFA World Cup drove the June-July spike. Football season, which overlaps other major leagues, starts a new peak now, and first-time users grew 22% YoY in the 2025 football season. Regulators and financial institutions are still working out how to treat event contracts. Under BofA's own framing they sit in a gray zone between entertainment and investing.
revenue_model: B2B: $2-5K/month pilot fees, then $0.25-0.60 per member per month. B2C: free P&L tool, $4.99/month for caps and alerts, and paid family co-guardian seats. Possible later add-on: aggregate, anonymized risk analytics for lenders.
non_obvious_insight: Self-serve gambling blocks fail because bettors do not classify themselves as gamblers, so a harm-reduction message framed as 'gambling addiction' gets ignored, while a return-on-investment statement speaks their mental model. BofA identified betting activity purely from ACH flows, which shows any bank can build the same detection. Working hypothesis, not verified because my search budget ran out: card merchant-category-code blocks used by many banks probably miss ACH-funded prediction-market deposits. Validate with two or three credit-union risk teams before building. Evidence: https://institute.bankofamerica.com/economic-insights/online-betting-platforms.html and its full PDF https://institute.bankofamerica.com/content/dam/economic-insights/online-betting-platforms.pdf (3x first-timers, recovery under 75 cents, 88% Gen Z plus Millennials, 20% see betting as investing, 59% median balance).
first_30_days: Week 1: compile a list of ACH originator and descriptor names for major sportsbooks, sweepstakes casinos and event-contract exchanges, and ship a client-side upload-a-CSV P&L calculator with a shareable result card. Week 2: seed it in Gen Z finance and sports-betting subreddits and Discords to collect real recovery-ratio numbers. Week 3: cold-email 30 credit unions near universities and military bases (member-financial-wellness and CUSO contacts) with the anonymized ratio data. Week 4: sign one or two paid pilots at $2-5K/month. Legal review of state gambling-related messaging rules is required before launch.

title: Baseline: Bank-Feed Proof of Displacement Costs
one_liner: An app that reconstructs a displaced family's 'normal' spending from pre-loss bank statements and computes the exact increase that Additional Living Expense coverage owes, in carrier-ready format.
customer: Public adjusters and disaster-recovery nonprofits (paying per file), and carriers or TPAs handling long-tail displaced-household claims (paying per active ALE file per month). Consumers use it free.
problem: ALE pays the increase over normal living costs, not the total, so proving it requires a baseline that almost no family has. Adjusters spend hours rebuilding it from memory and shoeboxes, families under-claim (groceries, laundry, mileage, pet boarding, storage, higher utilities) or document sloppily, and disputes turn ugly. With California's new smoke-damage law (AB 1795, effective Jan 1, 2027) barring insurers from cutting off ALE until the home is restored, thousands of standing-home households will run ALE claims for years with heavy documentation demands.
solution: A privacy-first tool that ingests 12 months of pre-loss bank or card data (via open-banking link or uploaded statements), builds a per-category baseline, then diffs it month by month against post-loss spending, matches receipts, and flags gaps the family can legitimately claim (extra mileage, meal delta, rented furniture, storage). Output is an ALE ledger with audit trail in the format desk adjusters actually accept, plus a deadline tracker for policy ALE time limits. Processing is on-device or in a private enclave, and the data is deleted after export.
why_now: More than 13,000 standing-home smoke claims from the Eaton and Palisades fires are still unresolved 20 months later, a lawsuit accuses Farmers' vendor of substandard assessments, and AB 1795 makes ALE duration a live issue. LLM parsing of messy statements and receipts is now cheap and accurate enough to be a product. Carriers are cutting adjusters (entry-level postings down about 50% since 2025) but ALE files still need documentation, so automation that delivers clean files is welcomed.
revenue_model: Public adjusters and recovery groups pay $99-$199 per file. Carriers and TPAs pay $30-$60 per active ALE file per month, or $75-$150 per closed file, in exchange for fewer touches and fewer complaints. Optional referral fees from moving, storage and rental-furniture vendors for legitimate, claimable purchases.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody in the industry records 'normal.' The claim's central number, the increase over normal, is unmeasured on the policyholder's side, and adjusters know most under-claiming is not a coverage denial but the family's inability to prove what they used to spend. Bank data is the only pre-loss record the insured always has.
first_30_days: Build a prototype that categorizes statement CSVs and PDFs into ALE categories and produces a monthly delta ledger. Offer it free to 10 Altadena and Palisades public adjusters and to two survivor-support networks in exchange for feedback and 20 anonymized-consent pilot files. Ask two carrier ALE desk managers to review the output format and sign a paid pilot at $50 per file for 200 files. Prepare a privacy policy and data-deletion promise, because trust is the product.

title: Port-Level IP Shield for Indie Brands
one_liner: A subscription that registers small brands' trademarks and copyrights with CBP, feeds officers product-identification guides, and turns port detentions into evidence and settlements against the importers.
customer: Indie consumer brands with $1-30M in revenue that get cloned: fashion, toys, beauty, pet, home goods and Shopify DTC brands. They pay a monthly subscription, plus a share of any enforcement settlements.
problem: Small brands fight knockoffs with Amazon Brand Registry and platform takedowns. Those work after the goods have landed and the listings are live. Most never use the cheapest lever, which is CBP itself. Recording a mark or copyright with CBP e-Recordation costs about $190 per class. CBP can then detain suspected counterfeit or lookalike shipments at the port, and the rights-holder can get photos, samples and importer details that support demand letters and lawsuits. In practice, small brands rarely record. When CBP does ask for authentication, the brand replies late, so the goods are released.
solution: 'Port Shield' handles recordation, builds a product-identification guide (photos, tells, label details, authorized-factory MID list) that officers can use, and monitors for CBP detention and seizure notices. It answers authentication requests within CBP's short response windows, and sets up lever-rule protection against gray-market goods where it applies. It also runs a port exposure scan: lookalike listings on marketplaces matched against public bill-of-lading data to find who is shipping them into LA/Long Beach. When CBP detains a shipment, it packages the importer identity and evidence for partner IP counsel to send demand letters, and takes a share of settlements.
why_now: Generative AI has made cloning product photos and standing up dupe storefronts nearly free, so knockoff volume against small brands is rising. The 2025 de minimis clampdown, and the statutory repeal scheduled for July 2027, push formerly parcel-shipped knockoffs into entries CBP can actually target and hold. Tariff-era entries also carry much richer line-level data, which improves targeting. Long Beach hit a record August of 919,992 TEUs, so port volume is not shrinking.
revenue_model: $750 setup, then $299-$799 a month by number of marks and product lines. Enforcement adds a 20-30% share of settlements, and IP counsel pays referral fees. A later tier sells port-level counterfeit intelligence to marketplaces and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: CBP can only hold what the rights-holder helps it verify. Officers see thousands of lookalikes and act on brands that have recorded marks, supplied identification guides and answered inquiries fast. Big brands have law firms doing this. Sub-$30M brands do not know the port is a free enforcement layer, and most of the relevant customs rules are written for lawyers, not founders.
first_30_days: Pick two crowded niches, such as LA-based apparel and accessories and Shopify beauty or pet. Run free port exposure scans on 30 brands by matching lookalikes to importers in public BOL data. Cold-email the brand owners with the scan attached. Sign 5-10 brands on a paid pilot, record their marks, and produce the first product-identification guides. Line up one IP law firm as the enforcement referral partner.

title: Off-the-Record Governance for AI Meeting Transcripts
one_liner: A policy layer over Zoom, Teams and Meet notetakers that decides what becomes 'the record'. It auto-pauses for privileged talk, purges verbatim transcripts once counsel-approved minutes are certified, and blocks unauthorized bots.
customer: General counsel and compliance leads at regulated mid-market companies with 200-5,000 employees, such as healthcare systems, fintechs, biotechs and defense contractors. Also law firms and corporate secretaries who run board minutes.
problem: AI notetakers made every meeting a verbatim, discoverable and error-prone transcript by default. A wrong attribution, such as 'we knew' instead of 'we know,' can become an exhibit. Third-party bots joining privileged calls raise waiver risk. Recording-consent class actions against AI notetaker vendors are rising, especially in all-party-consent states. General counsel have no control primitive between 'record everything' and 'ban notetakers.'
solution: A meeting-level record mode with three states: on the record, off the record and privileged. It is enforced through calendar tags, participant signals (a lawyer joins, so transcript is suppressed) and admin APIs for Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace. Verbatim transcripts carry retention timers (7-30 days, unless a legal hold applies). A named human designee approves a summary, which becomes the sole record with an attestation stamp modeled on a reporter's certificate. Add an audit log and a bot allow-list. It sits on top of the notetakers the company already uses.
why_now: Enterprises spent 2025-26 rolling out Copilot, Gemini and Zoom AI notes company-wide. Lawsuits over AI notetaker recording consent were filed in 2025. Regulators have punished off-channel record-keeping failures, so record governance is now a board-level topic. Legal teams are asking for controls now.
revenue_model: $6-$12 per user per month with a $25,000 annual minimum. An entry 'Record Risk Audit' as a fixed $5,000-$10,000 project that converts to the platform. A channel through employment and litigation law firms that advise clients on AI policy.
non_obvious_insight: Reporters live by one ritual, 'off the record,' a physical control (they stop writing) that AI notetakers lack. They also know that outside a proceeding a verbatim transcript is a liability, not an asset. Most companies are only now realizing they built a huge discoverable archive of casual speech.
first_30_days: Sell the $5,000 audit to 10 general counsel through ACC chapters and LinkedIn. Inventory each company's bot footprint from admin logs and deliver a policy template. Build a thin MVP using Microsoft Graph and Google admin APIs that flips transcription per meeting from calendar tags. Convert 3 audits into paid pilots.

title: Third-Party Maintenance for Orphaned Robots
one_liner: Like third-party server maintenance for IT, a spares-and-support contract for robots whose makers failed, were acquired or stopped supporting them.
customer: 3PLs, retailers, hospitals and factories running AMRs, storage systems and delivery robots that are out of warranty or whose vendors are gone, plus lenders and bankruptcy trustees holding stranded assets.
problem: Robotics funding is concentrating (Skild $14B, Physical Intelligence $11B, Figure $39B) while the long tail starves. Agility is pivoting toward wheels, and Serve's roughly $1.3k revenue per robot signals shakeout. Buyers can be left with multimillion-dollar fleets without updates or parts.
solution: Buy stranded inventory and spares from failed vendors, arrange source-code escrow or reverse-engineer key consumables, and offer annual per-robot support contracts with SLAs. Also sell certified refurbished units.
why_now: The 2025-26 funding boom is producing its first wave of failures and consolidation, while Amazon (1M+ robots, building its own robot factory) and Symbotic ($2.25B 2025 revenue) centralize the market. The orphan pool is growing now.
revenue_model: $1.5-4k per robot per year in support contracts, refurbished-unit sales, and escrow and trustee fees.
non_obvious_insight: In every hardware boom the durable second-derivative business is keeping the losers' machines running. Buyers pay to avoid stranded assets, and your spares moat grows with each vendor that fails.
first_30_days: Identify 3 wound-down or struggling robot vendors, get trustee quotes on inventory (often pennies on the dollar), and approach their 5 largest customers. Sign 2 support contracts and open a small depot near Memphis or the Inland Empire.

title: Agent-Access Terms Index for Enterprises
one_liner: A living database and alert feed of what the top 500 SaaS and data vendors allow, meter and prohibit when your AI agents touch their APIs and data.
customer: General counsel, procurement and IT platform leads at 100-5,000 employee companies deploying agents, plus their outside counsel. SaaS vendors are a later customer.
problem: Most insiders read the Ninth Circuit ruling (the user, not the agent vendor, accessed Amazon) as 'agents can roam free'. For enterprises it means the fight moves to contract, and the user's company is the bound party. Vendors are already moving. SAP restricts third-party AI agent access to its APIs, Slack has throttled non-Marketplace apps and banned persistent indexes, and ServiceNow throttles inbound agent traffic. Vendors are also adding agent-action meters. No one tracks any of this, so a company can breach terms at a dozen vendors and learn about it from a suspension or audit letter.
solution: Build a structured agent-use rights matrix for about 500 vendors: allowed, banned or priced, rate limits, indexing, retention and training clauses, and official connector alternatives. Add change detection on terms and API policy pages with plain-English diffs. Add a connector that maps your OAuth-connected apps and agent inventory to the matrix and flags conflicts. Include a clause library, negotiation playbooks and an audit-defense pack.
why_now: Platform lockdowns (SAP, Slack, ServiceNow) and per-agent-action pricing arrived in 2025-26, and the Ninth Circuit ruling (August 2026) made contract the main battleground. Amazon can still seek rehearing, which adds uncertainty buyers want tracked.
revenue_model: $1.5-5k/month subscriptions for legal and procurement teams, $8-25k fixed-fee exposure reviews and negotiation packages, and later vendor-side benchmarking.
non_obvious_insight: Contract terms are becoming the price list and permission system of the agent economy, and they sit in unstructured legalese nobody indexes. The index is also the negotiating leverage, because it shows a buyer what comparable vendors concede.
first_30_days: Have an LLM plus a contract lawyer parse the terms and API policies of the top 100 SaaS vendors. Publish a free Agent Rights Scorecard for 25 of them to generate inbound. Sign 5 design partners at $1.5k/month and offer a $8-15k agent contract exposure review.

title: PO-Backed Working Capital for Drone Sub-Tier
one_liner: A specialty lender that advances cash against Gauntlet-winner purchase orders to the motor, battery and casting shops that must ship first.
customer: Sub-tier suppliers (motors, ESCs, battery packs, castings, machined parts) with 10-200 staff feeding Drone Dominance winners and Navy autonomy programs; funded by a debt fund or family office.
problem: Insiders think mega-rounds fix the defense supply chain. The AIA-Bain study says no fit-for-purpose investment model exists for sub-tier makers. About 60,000 drones are being ordered, but the people who make the parts are too small for VC and too risky for banks.
solution: Underwrite the prime's award notice and delivery schedule, not the supplier's balance sheet. Offer PO advances, tooling leases and milestone-linked draws, with payment routed through the prime so the loan is self-liquidating. Public award data plus supplier-network mapping is the underwriting edge.
why_now: Gauntlet 2 (Sept 2026) produced roughly 60,000 units of orders. The Navy is stepping back to Series D-F co-investment. $14.6B of 2026 VC is going to primes, not the parts makers beneath them.
revenue_model: 1.5-3% per month on advances (10-15% blended yield), plus origination fees, plus small equity warrants on the best suppliers.
non_obvious_insight: The constraint is not capital in general but capital shaped like a receivable from a credit-worthy prime. Whoever routes payment through the prime turns a scary startup-supplier loan into near-prime credit.
first_30_days: Sign one debt-fund partner for a $5M pilot line. Pull award notices for the 19 Gauntlet 2 firms and cold-call their top 5 suppliers each. Fund 3 small POs against prime payment-assignment letters.

title: Royalty Marketplace for Expert Agent Skills
one_liner: Retired and displaced specialists package their procedures, judgment rubrics and worked examples as machine-loadable skill packs that companies' agents pull on demand, with per-run metering and royalties to the author.
customer: Enterprises and SMBs deploying agents in regulated or technical workflows pay $200-2,000 a month per seat or per run. Authors are displaced experts who earn royalties.
problem: Agents are competent generalists that fail on domain procedures (customs classification, prior-authorisation appeals, tax-exchange steps). Hourly expert gigs pay once, so expertise is consumed without ongoing income, and enterprises can't find vetted, tested procedures.
solution: A curated marketplace of skill packs in the open Agent Skills format (instructions, scripts and tests), each with an eval suite and author credentials, metered per invocation through an MCP gateway. Quality is scored on held-out test performance and versions update as rules change. Wedge: tariff and customs-compliance packs written by retired customs brokers.
why_now: The Agent Skills format (Oct 2025) and MCP are becoming standard across agent tools, tariff volatility since 2025 has created urgent demand for trade-compliance expertise, and experienced professionals are being displaced.
revenue_model: 25-30% take on subscriptions and per-run fees, plus enterprise private-skill hosting.
non_obvious_insight: Hourly data labor turns experts into a consumable, while royalties make them asset owners. A metered gateway makes value attributable, and the moat is trusted eval suites rather than the marketplace itself.
first_30_days: Recruit 8 retired customs brokers or trade-compliance professionals. Build 5 tested skill packs and an eval harness. Sell to 10 importers already using agents at $300 a month and measure error reduction.

title: Sub-Tier Surge Twin for the Industrial Base
one_liner: A digital twin of foundries, forges and motor makers that shows which supplier breaks first in a 180-day fight.
customer: Defense primes' supply-chain risk teams, private equity funds rolling up defense suppliers, DoD industrial-base offices, and sub-tier lenders.
problem: Leaders doubt they can sustain the 90-, 120- or 180-day fight and lack integrated supply-chain visibility. AIA-Bain identifies castings, forgings, sensors, semiconductors and solid rocket motors as bottlenecks. Private equity invests only $1-3B a year and is flying blind on capacity.
solution: Build a network model of sub-tier capacity from public and commercial data (facility permits, trade flows, workforce, energy use, certifications), calibrated by supplier surveys. Run agent-based surge scenarios to identify chokepoints and invest-or-acquire targets. Start with one commodity, castings and forgings.
why_now: The record defense funding wave is looking for bottlenecks to fund. Maven-scale AI targeting has raised concern about munition depth. Agentic simulation and cheap data enrichment make a 5-person twin feasible.
revenue_model: $60-250K per year per subscribing prime or fund, plus deal-sourcing fees on roll-up acquisitions.
non_obvious_insight: The people who will pay first are private equity funds hunting acquisition targets, not the Pentagon. The twin's early output is a target list for whoever wants to roll up the base.
first_30_days: Map 300 casting and forging plants from public data and publish a bottleneck brief. Present to 5 PE funds and 3 primes' supply-chain teams. Sign one paid pilot for a commodity view.
